note: General, widely documented customs. Practices vary by region, family and generation, so treat these as starting points, not rules.

en.name: English

greetings.use: A very formal greeting; the usual reply is to repeat it.
Said on a first meeting, usually with a handshake.

etiquette: A handshake is the usual greeting in formal and business settings; friends often just say hi.
Small talk (weather, travel, weekend plans) is a normal way to start a conversation.
Please, thank you and sorry are used very often, even for small things.
do: Queue politely and wait your turn.
Be on time for meetings and appointments.
dont: Do not push in front of a queue.
Avoid asking strangers about their salary or age.
Do not assume all English speakers share one accent or culture.

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.about: Celebrated across many English-speaking countries with family meals and gifts.

festivals.name: Thanksgiving (USA)
festivals.about: A family meal and a day of gratitude.

festivals.about: Fireworks and barbecues.

festivals.name: Burns Night (Scotland)
festivals.about: Poetry and a supper in honour of the poet Robert Burns.

hi.name: Hindi

greetings.use: The everyday greeting for hello and goodbye, said with palms pressed together.

etiquette: Greet with namaste, palms together and a slight nod. A handshake is common in business, but wait for the other person to offer.
Use the respectful form 'āp' with elders and people you have just met.
Take your shoes off before entering a home or a temple.
do: Accept tea or food when it is offered; hospitality matters.
Use your right hand to give, receive and eat.
dont: Do not point your feet at people or at sacred objects.
Do not wear shoes inside a temple or many homes.

festivals.name: Diwali
festivals.when: Autumn (October or November; date follows the lunar calendar)
festivals.about: The festival of lights, with lamps, sweets and family gatherings.

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.about: The festival of colours.

festivals.name: Republic Day
festivals.about: Marks the day the Constitution of India came into effect.

festivals.name: Independence Day
festivals.about: Flag hoisting and celebrations across the country.

festivals.name: Gandhi Jayanti
festivals.about: The birthday of Mahatma Gandhi.

es.name: Spanish
etiquette: Spanish has a formal 'usted' and an informal 'tú'. Use usted with elders and strangers until invited to switch.
In Spain, friends often greet with two kisses on the cheeks; customs differ in Latin America, where one kiss or a handshake is common.
In Spain, lunch is the main meal and is eaten later than in many countries, often after 2 pm, and dinner is late as well.
do: Greet people when you enter a shop or a room.
Use usted until the other person suggests tú.
Allow time for conversation; meals and visits are social.
dont: Do not assume every Spanish-speaking country has the same food or customs.
Do not rush a meal; eating is social.
Avoid reducing a whole country to a stereotype.

festivals.name: Día de Muertos (Mexico)
festivals.about: Families remember loved ones with altars and flowers.

festivals.name: San Fermín (Pamplona, Spain)
festivals.about: Known for the running of the bulls.

festivals.name: La Tomatina (Buñol, Spain)
festivals.about: A giant tomato fight.

festivals.name: Las Fallas (Valencia, Spain)
festivals.about: Large papier-mâché figures are displayed and then burned.

festivals.name: Día de Reyes
festivals.about: Three Kings Day, when children traditionally receive gifts in Spain and many Latin American countries.

fr.name: French

greetings.use: Hello / good day. Expected when entering a shop.

etiquette: Say bonjour when you enter a shop or office, and au revoir when you leave.
French has formal 'vous' and informal 'tu'. Use vous with strangers and elders.
Friends often greet with 'la bise', light kisses on the cheeks. The number differs by region.
do: Greet first, then ask your question.
Use vous until invited to say tu.
Say 'bon appétit' before a meal and wait for others to start.
dont: Do not skip the greeting and go straight to a request.
Avoid asking people about their salary.
Do not assume everyone will switch to English; try a few words of French first.

festivals.name: Beaujolais Nouveau day
festivals.about: The release of the year's new wine.

zh.name: Mandarin

greetings.use: A polite hello for elders or customers.

etiquette: Family names come first: in Wang Fang, Wang is the family name.
Offer and receive business cards and gifts with both hands.
Elders are greeted first and treated with extra respect.
do: Use both hands for cards and gifts.
Accept a drink or snack offered by a host.
Learn the tones; they change the meaning of a word.
dont: Do not stick chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
Avoid giving a clock as a gift; the words for it sound like a word associated with funerals.
Avoid sensitive topics such as politics when you have just met someone.
